learned.head: Speed
learned.text: On weekdays, buses averaged 7.3 mph with stops included over the last 4 comparable weeks (Aug. 31 to Sept. 27), against 7.5 mph in the first 4 (July 6 to Aug. 2). The trend across all 11 comparable weeks points down, about 0.2 mph end to end. September is usually slower than August: the MTA's own figure fell from August to September in 6 of the 7 years since 2019. Weekends ran faster, 8.0 mph recently.

learned.head: Checked against the MTA
learned.text: Ranked from slowest to fastest, the 342 routes come out in nearly the same order as in the MTA's own figures for August 2026. The MTA's figure for the typical local route falls between the tracker's two measures: speed with stops reads 7% slower, moving speed 6% faster.

learned.head: The day
learned.text: Weekday buses move fastest around 10 p.m. (8.7 mph) and slowest around 2 p.m. (6.4 mph). The 7-to-10 a.m. rush averages 7.2 mph, faster than mid-afternoon.

learned.head: Boroughs
learned.text: Among local routes, Staten Island is the fastest at 10.9 mph and Manhattan the slowest at 5.4 mph. The slowest busy route is the M42 at 4.2 mph.

learned.head: Riders
learned.text: Weekday boardings counted by the MTA's passenger counters averaged 1.29 million over the three months through August 2026, against 1.36 million in the twelve months before and 1.42 million in the same three months a year earlier. The counters are partial: they ran only 9% above paid fare taps in those three months, though the MTA estimates about half of local riders don't pay.

learned.head: A change of method
learned.text: Until October 2026 this page reported moving speed, which leaves out time stopped at stops and lights. Recently that measure read 8.3 mph on weekdays, about 1 mph above speed with stops. Every week was recomputed the new way, so the charts compare like with like.

learned.head: Ahead of the MTA
learned.text: The MTA has not yet published September 2026. If its headline figure moves the way the tracker did, it will come in near 8.31 mph, 0.19 below August 2026's 8.50. Made this way, the forecast for August 2026 would have missed by 0.02 mph.

official.intro: The tracker makes its own estimates from GPS positions. Here they are set beside what the MTA publishes, which runs about six weeks behind. The latest month both sources cover is August 2026.

nowcast.text: The MTA has not yet published September 2026. If its headline figure moves the way the tracker did, it will come in near 8.31 mph, 0.19 below August 2026's 8.50. Made this way, the forecast for August 2026 would have missed by 0.02 mph.

metrics.label: Local routes, whole system
metrics.why: Built the same way on both sides: local, limited and Select Bus Service routes each count once; every hour from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. counts equally; weekdays and weekends are averaged separately and blended 5 to 2. The tracker's figure includes time stopped and reads below the MTA's; the next two rows say why. The MTA's headline figure, which weights routes by the miles they run and covers all hours, was 8.5 mph.

metrics.label: Typical local route, speed with stops
metrics.why: Median across 265 local, limited and Select Bus Service routes, weekdays. Straight lines between GPS fixes about 40 seconds apart cut corners on turning routes, which makes it read low.

metrics.label: Typical local route, moving speed only
metrics.why: The tracker's original measure, which drops readings under 0.5 mph. Leaving out time stopped makes it read fast.

metrics.label: Staten Island express (SIM)
metrics.why: Median across 27 SIM routes, speed with stops. Express buses are kept out of the tracker's index.

metrics.label: Weekday riders
metrics.why: Both are MTA numbers. The first comes from passenger counters on board; the second is the MTA's daily bus ridership estimate. The riders chart above uses the counters.

flags.head: Routes line up almost exactly
flags.text: Rank the 342 routes both sources cover from slowest to fastest, and the two lists nearly match (rank correlation 0.99, where 1 is identical).
flags.detail: For comparing routes with each other, the tracker and the MTA tell the same story.

flags.head: The MTA figure falls between the tracker's two measures
flags.text: On the typical local route, moving-only speed reads 6% faster than the MTA, and speed with stops reads 7% slower. B41: 6.6 mph with stops, 7.7 moving, 6.9 MTA; M15+: 7.5 mph with stops, 8.6 moving, 7.8 MTA; BX19: 5.5 mph with stops, 6.6 moving, 5.6 MTA.
flags.detail: Moving speed leaves out time stopped, so it reads high. Speed with stops measures straight lines between GPS fixes about 40 seconds apart, which cut corners on routes that turn, so it reads low. Both rank routes the same way and move with the MTA from month to month, which is what the tracker is for.

flags.head: Staten Island express buses read slower here
flags.text: SIM express routes read 13% slower than the MTA. SIM22: 17.7 mph here, 21.2 MTA.
flags.detail: Not yet explained. Candidates include positions that refresh less often on highway stretches. Express routes are kept out of the index for this reason.

flags.head: Month to month, the two move together
flags.text: From July 2026 to August 2026 the tracker moved +0.0 mph and the MTA, built the same way, +0.0 mph.
flags.detail: Moves of a tenth or two are within the noise of either source.

flags.head: The MTA's two ridership counts disagree
flags.text: Over the last 12 months, the passenger-counter figure ran anywhere from 96% to 112% of the MTA's daily bus ridership count.
flags.detail: So a month-to-month change in riders depends on which count you use. Say which one.
